::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Using limit laws while calculating the difference quotient?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1088427/using-limit-laws-while-calculating-the-difference-quotient), asked by [FigureItOut](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/190098/figureitout) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-01-02; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I'm trying to calculate the difference quotient of $f(x) = x|x|$ to calculate to derivative at $x=0$.
>
> Now when I try to do: $\lim_{h\to0} f(x)=\frac{(x+h)|x+h|-x|x|}{h}$ it just seems too complicated to calculate.
>
>
> I even tried this:
>
> $$\lim_{h\to0}{ \frac{x+h-x}{h}} \lim_{h\to0}{ \frac{|x+h|-|x|}{h}}$$
> Is this legal?
>
> Even so, I still don't know how to calculate to right limit.
>
> How do you calculate the difference quotient of this function?:|
:::

The really special behavior of this this function is at zero, so rather than do something for general $x$ and then “plug in” $x=0$, it's easier to start with $x=0$.  By the definition of the derivative, then by the definition of $f$:
$$\begin{align*}
   f'(0) &= \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(h)}{h} \\
         &= \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{h\left|h\right|}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} |h| = 0
\end{align*}$$
